clue.text: Regret hiding key for release

indicators.note: Something hiding has been put where it cannot be seen, so the word beside it closes over the letters and keeps them out of sight.

blocks.note: to rue a decision is to regret it
Esc is the key at the top left corner of a keyboard

explanation.surface: Someone smothering their regret over the key that would have set a prisoner free.
explanation.walkthrough: The key is the one on a keyboard rather than one that turns in a lock, and Esc is the label printed on it. 'For' is doing nothing but joining the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A rescue is a deliverance from danger or captivity, which is release in the sense of being set free rather than letting go.

clue.text: What’s at stake climbing volcano

indicators.note: Something climbing is heading upwards, and in a down entry that means the letters are read from the foot of the column back to the top.

blocks.note: the ante is the stake every player puts in before a hand is dealt, and it goes up the column

explanation.surface: The risk a walker takes in climbing an active volcano.
explanation.walkthrough: An ante is the compulsory bet laid before the cards come out, which is where the phrase 'upping the ante' comes from. 'Climbing' only reverses because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the volcano on the east coast of Sicily, the tallest active one in Europe, so it stands for the general word by example.

clue.text: Regime change due to pact being broken

indicators.note: What is broken has come apart into pieces, and pieces that have come apart do not go back together in the order they were in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A government toppling because the agreement holding it together has collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes the answer as well as hiding it, which is what makes the fodder so hard to spot. 'Due to' reads as the phrase that explains a cause and is five of the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A coup d'état is the sudden seizure of power from a sitting government, which is regime change brought about by force rather than by an election.

clue.text: Surviving navigation aid lacking its lid

indicators.note: To lack something is to be missing it, so the word just named goes without the letter the clue points to next.

blocks.note: a sextant is the brass instrument that fixes a ship's position by the angle of a star above the horizon
the letter sitting on top of the column, lifted off

explanation.surface: An old ship's instrument that still works despite having lost its cover.
explanation.walkthrough: A sextant was how sailors found their latitude before satellites, by sighting the sun or a star down to the horizon. The lid is the top letter because this entry runs downwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extant is still in existence — an extant manuscript is one that has come down to us — so it has survived where others did not.

clue.text: I can’t wait to see dams shut off

indicators.note: Milk or meat that has gone off has turned into something else, and letters that turn come out in an order they were not given in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A campaigner longing for the day the hydroelectric dams are finally closed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I can't wait' reads as eagerness and means the opposite sort of impatience — the speaker has no time and is leaving. 'Shut off' looks like one phrase and splits across fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Must dash' is what you say when there is no time left to stay, the sense of not being able to wait that means going now rather than being excited.

clue.text: Core season broadcast provides extra weight

blocks.note: the core of anything is its middle
to season timber or a cask is to let it age
to broadcast seed is to scatter it across the field, which is to spread it

explanation.surface: A programme aired at the height of the season carrying more importance than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcasting was a sower's word centuries before it was a radio one: seed thrown wide across a field was broadcast. Three separate words of the surface each hand over a different chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-age spread is the thickening round the waist that arrives in a person's forties and fifties — extra weight, and exactly where it settles.

clue.text: Demonstrated about empty airfield that’s obscured

indicators.note: What goes about something goes round it, so the letters just named open up and take the next chunk inside.
An empty container has nothing between its walls, so the word keeps its first and last letters and loses everything in between.

blocks.note: to demonstrate a gadget is to show it, and this is the past tense to match
the first and last letters of AirfielD, all that is left once the middle goes

explanation.surface: Protesters making their case about a deserted airfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrated' reads as marching with placards and means showed. Emptying a word down to its outer letters is worth learning — 'empty', 'hollow' and 'vacant' all ask for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shadowed corner is one the light does not reach, so whatever is in it is obscured — hidden by shade rather than by anything solid.

clue.text: AI contributes occasional parts to DVD showing Michelangelo’s masterpiece

indicators.note: To contribute parts to something is to put them in, and parts that come occasionally come at intervals — so these letters go in one at a time, at alternate places.

blocks.note: the three letters of the disc format, keeping their order and taking the odd places
the two letters of artificial intelligence, split between the second place and the fourth

explanation.surface: Artificial intelligence credited here and there on a disc about a famous statue.
explanation.walkthrough: Most containers drop a chunk into a single gap; this one splits two letters between two gaps, which is what 'occasional' is buying. Michelangelo's marble youth stands in the Accademia in Florence.
explanation.definitionFit: David is Michelangelo's marble colossus of the shepherd boy squaring up to Goliath, the statue that made his name and the one he is best known for.

clue.text: Lyric producer, one misquoting what Spooner said?

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was the Oxford don remembered for trading the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so anything he said arrives with those noises swapped.

blocks.note: to misquote is to get the words wrong; 'wrong' opens on an R sound, and taking the S coming the other way that noise is spelt this way
the one here is a citer, somebody quoting a source; handed the R the other word gave up, the noise is spelt this way

explanation.surface: Someone garbling a quotation the way the Reverend Spooner used to garble his sentences.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'wrong citer' aloud and let the R and the S at the fronts change places. The W never moves at all, because it is silent in both spellings.
explanation.definitionFit: A songwriter produces the lyric — the words a singer sings — so the definition names the job by its output rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Humiliated – without a means to be protected

indicators.note: To be without something is to be missing it, so the word named here goes on lacking the letter the clue picks out.

blocks.note: a loft or a cable kept safe from heat or current has been insulated
the single letter lifted out of that word

explanation.surface: A humiliating draught, felt because there is no lagging anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the only punctuation and it hides the join: everything to its right is wordplay. 'Without a' looks like the start of an ordinary phrase and is an instruction to drop one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To be insulted is to have been spoken to contemptuously, which leaves you humiliated — the loss of face is the whole point of the insult.

clue.text: First appearance of commercial release

blocks.note: the commercial between television programmes is an ad
to vent steam or a grievance is to release it

explanation.surface: The day a new record or film first goes on general sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial release' reads as one phrase about a product reaching the shops, and the two words belong to different chunks of the wordplay. Advent is also the church season of waiting before Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: The advent of something is its arrival or coming into use — the advent of the mobile phone — so it names a first appearance.

clue.text: Advice given to climbers – appear optimistic!

definitions.note: The first half names the phrase rather than being a synonym for it: what climbers are told is this very instruction, which is how a whole spoken sentence gets defined.

blocks.note: the literal reading: on a rock face, keep your eyes off the drop below you
the second reading is about a face, where looking down is looking glum

explanation.surface: A mountaineer being told to keep their chin up on the way to the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same three words said to two different people. On a rock face it is literal — keep your eyes off the drop — and in the second it is the face you are wearing.
explanation.definitionFit: On a cliff it is the standard warning against looking at the drop; of a face, looking down means looking glum, so refusing to is looking optimistic.

clue.text: Very eager to describe what it’s like being dead?

definitions.note: The second half is a description rather than a synonym — being dead is being without breath — and the question mark is the setter marking the joke.

blocks.note: the plain reading: the state of someone panting with excitement and anticipation
the joke reading, taking the word at its parts: no breath at all

explanation.surface: Somebody asking, a little too keenly, what dying actually feels like.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the everyday figure — breathless with excitement, breathless anticipation — where nobody is short of air at all. The second takes the word apart literally instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Breathless covers both: panting with eagerness, and, read exactly as its parts say, having no breath, which is the plain condition of the dead.

clue.text: Dry, although fed by river

indicators.note: A lake fed by a stream takes that water into itself, so the word here opens and takes the letter in.

blocks.note: but and although both introduce the contrast that follows
R is how river is shortened on maps and in gazetteers

explanation.surface: A channel that stays dry even though a river runs into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Brut on a label means the driest grade of champagne, drier than sec despite what the French word suggests. The river is the single-letter one from atlases, not a named one, so nothing longer is hiding here.
explanation.definitionFit: Brut is the grade of champagne fermented out to almost no residual sugar, which is what dry means when it is said of wine.

clue.text: Primate has short service providing drink

indicators.note: Something cut short stops before it should, so the word this describes gives up the letter it ends on.

blocks.note: apes are the primates — chimpanzees, gorillas, orang-utans
a church service is a rite, here docked of its final E
'providing it rains' and 'if it rains' say the same thing

explanation.surface: A quick church service at which the clergy lay on drinks afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: A primate is also the archbishop who heads a province, which is the churchman the surface wants and the zoo animal the wordplay needs. 'Providing' looks like a verb and is the conjunction if.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is the small drink taken before a meal to sharpen the appetite — a vermouth, a sherry, a kir.

clue.text: Oops, I got muddled about information that makes it true

definitions.note: The answer is a Latin adverbial phrase and the definition is the English clause it stands in for — the fact by itself settles the matter.

indicators.note: Something muddled has been stirred together, and letters stirred together do not stay in the order they arrived in.
To go about something is to go round it, so the jumbled letters open up and close over the chunk named next.

blocks.note: the five letters of the exclamation and the pronoun, stirred into this order
a fact is a piece of hard information

explanation.surface: A flustered speaker apologising for tangling up the details.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of the muddling and is a separate instruction that prises the jumble apart. The comma after 'Oops' reads as punctuation and sits inside the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipso facto means by that very fact: the fact on its own is enough to settle the matter, with no further argument needed.

clue.text: As it happens, doing something that will satisfy

blocks.note: a broadcast going out as it happens, with no recording in between, is live
asking what somebody is up to is asking what they are doing

explanation.surface: By the way, there is a job going that somebody would find rewarding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As it happens' reads as the conversational 'by the way' and is the broadcaster's term for an unrecorded transmission. The enumeration warns you early that three separate words are coming.
explanation.definitionFit: To live up to a promise or a reputation is to meet what was expected of it, which is satisfying a demand rather than pleasing a person.

clue.text: Leaf tips damaged? It’s happened to you before

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and the definition is a sentence about it: a past life is precisely the one whose events happened to you before this one.

indicators.note: What is damaged has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape do not keep the arrangement they came in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A gardener noticing that the ends of the leaves have gone brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' is almost always the first-letters instruction, and here it is ordinary fodder — the brown ends of the leaves. The definition is reincarnation, spelt out as a whole sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A past life is the earlier existence reincarnation claims you lived before this one, so everything in it is something that happened to you before.

clue.text: Measure part of flight

blocks.note: the plain reading: a single action taken towards an end, one of several a government might announce
a flight is the run of stairs between two landings, and its parts are the treads

explanation.surface: An instruction to measure one section of a staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: A flight is the unbroken run of stairs between two landings, so its parts are the things you tread on. The other half is the sense in 'take steps to prevent it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A step is an action taken towards an end — 'take steps' — which is exactly a measure; it is also each tread in a run of stairs.

clue.text: Crowds reported in stores

indicators.note: What is reported reaches you by word of mouth, so you want the word as it sounds and not as it is spelt.

blocks.note: hordes are great crowds of people, and the two spellings are said exactly alike

explanation.surface: News of big crowds turning up at the shops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In stores' reads as one phrase about shops and then splits: only the last word is the definition. The two spellings are exact homophones in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a store laid by and kept back — coins buried in a field, tins at the back of a cupboard — so the plural answers to 'stores'.

clue.text: Destroy evidence that’s impossible to crack

blocks.note: to shatter something is to destroy it by breaking it into pieces
proof is the evidence that settles the question

explanation.surface: Getting rid of the evidence in a case nobody has managed to break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroy evidence' reads as one criminal act and is two unrelated words of wordplay. The -proof ending of the answer has nothing to do with evidence: it is the sense meaning able to withstand.
explanation.definitionFit: Shatterproof glass is made so that it cannot be broken — a windscreen, a phone screen — which is what 'impossible to crack' promises.

clue.text: Number present as resistance rises a notch

indicators.note: Resistance is R to a physicist, and asking that R to rise a notch moves it one place up the column, swapping it with the letter above.

blocks.note: anybody who was present at the meeting was there

explanation.surface: A reading taken as the resistance in a circuit climbs one step.
explanation.walkthrough: This is not a free jumble: one named letter shifts one place, and everything else stays put. 'Present' is the adjective for being in attendance, not a gift and not a tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Three is one of the counting numbers, so the definition just names the class it belongs to — the one word of the clue that is not an instruction.

clue.text: Leaders of Britain always look desperate – that’s plain

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so each word named after this gives up only the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words, taken in order

explanation.surface: A country whose politicians are looking more frantic by the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' reads as the people running the country and means the letters at the front of the words after it. The dash is the join and does no work in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bald statement is one given with nothing added to soften it, the same figure of speech as a head with no covering on it.

clue.text: Rent doubled? Get really angry

indicators.note: Something doubled is taken twice over, so the word in front of it is used a second time, in a second and unrelated sense.

blocks.note: a flat rented out to a tenant has been let
on its second turn the same word is the tear sense: a rent in a sail is a rip

explanation.surface: A tenant reacting to the rent going up twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent is two unrelated words wearing the same spelling: the past of letting out, and a tear in cloth. The question mark is the setter admitting the second one is a stretch of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To let rip is to stop holding back, most often a burst of temper, which is getting really angry rather than merely showing it.

clue.text: Official in Brussels mixed up our crate

indicators.note: What is mixed up has had its contents stirred together, and letters stirred together come out in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A customs man in Brussels rummaging through a crate of ours.
explanation.walkthrough: Brussels is where the European Commission and Council sit, so naming the city names the EU civil service rather than a place of work. 'Mixed up' earns its keep in the surface too: the crate has been turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: A eurocrat is a career civil servant of the European Union institutions, which is what being an official in Brussels amounts to.

clue.text: Heavenly body of flower copied regularly

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval rather than all together, so you take every second one across the word.

blocks.note: the aster is the late-summer daisy of cottage borders
the second, fourth and sixth letters of cOpIeD

explanation.surface: A bloom that keeps being reproduced, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' in a cryptic is usually a river, something that flows; this time it really is a plant. Every-other-letter clues can start at the first letter or the second, and this one starts at the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is one of the rocky bodies circling the sun between Mars and Jupiter, so it is a heavenly body named by example.

clue.text: Modest clothing uneven and substandard

indicators.note: Clothes go round the body inside them, so this word wraps itself about the letters the clue names next.

blocks.note: a shy person is modest about coming forward
uneven numbers are the odd ones, those that will not halve

explanation.surface: Plain clothes that hang badly and were poorly made in the first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modest' in talk about clothing means covering up, which is the surface; the wordplay wants the retiring person instead. 'Uneven' is arithmetic here, not a complaint about the hem.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy goods are cheaply and carelessly made, which is substandard — the word began as the waste wool that such cloth was bulked out with.
